content: Linaria vulgaris, commonly known as Common Toadflax, is a species of the genus Linaria. It is native to a wide range of regions across Europe and northern Asia, extending from the United Kingdom in the west to Spain in the south, and further east to eastern Siberia and western China. This plant is a perennial species characterized by its short, spreading roots and upright to decumbent stems that can grow to a height of 15–90 cm. Its leaves are slender, thread-like, and exhibit a glaucous blue-green coloration, measuring 2–6 cm in length and 1–5 mm in width. The flowers of Linaria vulgaris resemble those of the snapdragon and are 25–33 mm in length. They are pale yellow in color, with the exception of the lower lip, which is orange. These flowers are arranged in dense terminal racemes and bloom from mid-summer to mid-autumn. The fruit of the plant is a globose capsule, measuring 5–11 mm in length and 5–7 mm in width, and it contains numerous small seeds. Ecology Linaria vulgaris is commonly found in ruderal habitats, such as roadsides, dunes, and disturbed or cultivated lands. Due to the largely closed structure of its flowers, pollination requires robust insects, particularly bees and bumblebees (species of the genus Bombus). The plant serves as a food source for a variety of insects, including the Sweet-Gale Moth (Acronicta euphorbiae), Mouse Moth (Amphipyra tragopoginis), Silver Y (Autographa gamma), Calophasia lunula, Gorgone Checkerspot (Charidryas gorgone carlota), Toadflax Pug (Eupithecia linariata), Satyr Pug (Eupithecia satyrata), Falseuncaria ruficiliana, Bog Fritillary (Proclossiana eunomia eunomia), Pyrrhia umbra, Brown Rustic (Rusina ferruginea), and Stenoptilia bipunctidactyla. Cultivation and Uses Although Linaria vulgaris is most commonly regarded as a weed, it is occasionally cultivated for its use as a cut flower, as its blooms are long-lasting in vases. Similar to snapdragons (Antirrhinum), it is often grown in children’s gardens for its snapping flowers, which can be made to talk by squeezing the base of the corolla. The plant thrives in well-drained soil but is otherwise adaptable to a variety of growing conditions. Other Names Linaria acutiloba Fisch. ex Rchb. is a synonym for this species. Due to its widespread growth as a weed, Linaria vulgaris has acquired numerous colloquial names, including brideweed, bridewort, butter and eggs, butter haycocks, bread and butter, bunny haycocks, bunny mouths, calf’s snout, Continental weed, dead men’s bones, devil’s flax, devil’s flower, doggies, dragon bushes, eggs and bacon, eggs and butter, false flax, flaxweed, fluellen, gallweed, gallwort, imprudent lawyer, impudent lawyer, Jacob’s ladder, lion’s mouth, monkey flower, North American ramsted, rabbit flower, rancid, ransted, snapdragon, wild flax, wild snapdragon, wild tobacco, yellow rod, and yellow toadflax.
